linkedin.title: AI search is changing how we read the news, and it is not just about speed.
linkedin.body:
For years, finding information meant typing keywords into a box and scrolling through a list of blue links. You had to do the heavy lifting: reading multiple articles, cross-referencing facts, and forming your own conclusion.

Now, AI search is shifting that dynamic. It can synthesize information across sources to give you a direct answer. This is a massive improvement for efficiency, but it changes the relationship we have with journalism. When an AI summarizes the news for you, the nuance of the original reporting can sometimes get lost in the middle.

We believe the future of news isn't just about getting an answer faster. It is about getting the right answer from sources you trust, presented in a way that respects your time and intelligence. The goal of technology should be to help you stay informed, not just to feed you a summary.

True personalization means connecting you with the stories that actually matter to your world, rather than just serving up what the algorithm thinks is popular.

story_card.headline: Space dust reveals how our sun was born
story_card.standfirst: Scientists found a 4.6 billion year old fossil record inside ancient meteorites.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text: Researchers found space dust inside meteorites that dates back 4.6 billion years.

steps.label: How we got here
steps.text: This dust acts like a fossil record, preserving clues from the sun's very early days.

steps.label: Why it matters
steps.text: It proves magnetism played a key role in the formation of our entire solar system.

steps.label: What to watch
steps.text: Future studies will analyze more meteorite samples to learn about early solar history.

story_card.caption:
Scientists are using 4.6 billion year old space dust to understand how the infant sun formed.

This discovery gives us a rare look at the magnetic forces that shaped our solar system. By studying these ancient meteorites, researchers are piecing together the story of our sun's earliest moments.

Does the idea of finding history in space dust make you feel small or connected to the universe?
